stepInfo.context: Context is the ground everything stands on: who you are, what you offer, for whom — and the market you move in. Every later recommendation from George rests on these facts; without solid context, values, archetype and tagline would be guesses instead of derivations.
stepInfo.pvm: The compass of your brand: the purpose says why you exist. The vision, where you are headed. The mission, how you get there. Together they are the yardstick for every decision — from the price list to the Instagram post.
stepInfo.architecture: Brand architecture sorts your family of brands: does everything appear under one brand, do products carry names of their own — and who lends trust to whom? From three switches George derives a model and turns it into a naming rule every future offer can be measured against.
stepInfo.values: Values are the rules of conduct of your brand: they say how you decide when it gets uncomfortable. In the Brand Foundation they are the hinge between purpose (why you exist) and archetype & voice (how you sound) — every later design and copy decision is measured against them.
stepInfo.archetype: The archetype gives your brand a recognisable character — a pattern people understand intuitively (the sage, the explorer, the caregiver …). The voice derives from it: how you sound, what you talk about and what you never do. That way everyone on the team writes as if the same person were writing.
stepInfo.manifesto: The manifesto condenses the whole foundation into one text with a stance — the piece you can read out loud: on the website, in the pitch, when onboarding new people. It grows out of purpose, values and voice, not the other way round.
stepInfo.verbal: The tagline is the one line next to your name; the messaging is the set of core messages behind it — what you tell whom so it sticks. Both build on the foundation: without clarified values, every tagline sounds arbitrary.
stepInfo.naming: Whether it is a new brand or a test bench for the existing name: here the name is measured against the foundation — does it fit purpose, values and archetype? Plus the sober checks: is it available, is it pronounceable, does it work in English too?
stepInfo.result: The result bundles every confirmed decision of the foundation into your brand document — with a direction for everything that follows. From here you move on to design, copy and the public face; and the more honest the chapters before, the more the result can carry.
stepInfo.dna: Before colour and type there is a direction. Frida reads your foundation and — if you bring any — your references, and turns both into ten named properties of your form instead of a mood.
stepInfo.color: Your colours do not come from a catalogue: a base colour is derived from archetype and values, and from it a checked light and dark ramp with accessible contrast pairs.
stepInfo.type: Type is voice in form. Your tone leads to a pair for headings and body text, plus sizes, hierarchy and the rules for where each cut applies.
stepInfo.mark: The direction of your mark — wordmark, monogram or symbol — with a brief and set examples. A draft is a draft, not a finished, protectable logo.
stepInfo.imagery: How your brand looks when it is not speaking: photography style, illustration and icons — with do & don’t to feel rather than a list of adjectives.
stepInfo.motion: Motion with character: pace and transitions, whether your mark moves — and what happens for someone who asked for reduced motion.
stepInfo.nomenclature: When a brand grows, every new thing gets a name — and without a pattern it gets just any name. Otto derives one naming pattern per kind of thing from your brand architecture and turns it into rules every future name can be measured against.
stepInfo.aiguide: AI already writes along. Here you settle what it may produce in your name, who approves it and which guardrails apply — tone, banned words, spellings. Nika derives all of it from your voice; nothing is invented.
stepInfo.presskit: Almost finished from what is already there: boilerplates, tagline, marks. Two things still need a human — which facts may travel publicly and who the press contact is.

b.purpose: Purpose is the WHY: the reason you exist beyond making money. Vision is the WHERE TO, mission is the HOW — three sentences, three jobs. Patagonia's purpose does not sell jackets; it wants to save the planet.
b.vision: The vision describes the world once you have succeeded — a picture, not a target figure. It may sit ten years out and still has to give direction today.
b.mission: The mission says what you do every day to get there — concrete enough that a new colleague could act on it. Purpose is why, vision is where to, mission is how.
b.positioningCategory: Positioning is the place you claim in someone's head: a category, and the people for whom you are the first choice within it. Without a category people still compare you — just without your say in it.

b2.model: Four models: branded house (one brand carries everything), sub-brands, endorsed brands, house of brands (brands without a visible parent). Each buys a different kind of trust, and each has a price.

c.candidates: Values are rules of behaviour that are allowed to cost money — not poster words. Survey after survey finds that most employees cannot name their own company's values; that is what happens when the words were picked for their sound.
c.final: Three to five is the working range: fewer says nothing, more nobody remembers. Take the ones you would defend in a bad week, not the ones that read well.

d.pairs: The archetype is your brand's character — it steers voice, imagery and effect. You don't pick it off a list: it comes out of comparisons, because a decision between two feelings is more honest than a menu of twelve.
d.primary: Twelve archetypes in four groups; you get a primary and a secondary one. The primary sets the tone, the secondary keeps it from turning into a cliché.
d.gapReveal: Here your self-image meets the picture your current appearance sends out. A gap is not a mistake — it is the most useful thing on this page, and it gets named plainly instead of smoothed over.

e.statements: A manifesto takes a stand: it should attract the right people and put off the wrong ones. The openers are scaffolding — cross out whatever sounds borrowed and keep what you would say out loud.
e.manifesto: A mission explains, a manifesto commits. It is written to be read aloud, so shorter and sharper almost always wins.

f.nameType: There are nine kinds of names — descriptive, invented, metaphorical and so on. Choose the kind first, then brainstorm: a mixed list always collapses into the safest option.
f.taste: The name is the most repeated element of a brand — it has to be sayable, memorable and protectable. What you love about other people's names says more about your taste than any list of adjectives.
f.checks: The more invented a name, the more protectable it is. What you see here are indicators from public registries and from DNS — general information, not legal advice. Talk to a trademark lawyer before you commit.

what.honest: This is a maturity level, not a report card: it says where you stand today and what would be next.
what.f1Body: Each with a fixed rule from 0 to 2. None of it is taste.
what.f2Body: From distinctiveness to craft, each with its own weight.
what.f3Body: One number with a band that you can compare with today a year from now.

why.title: Your brand takes shape in other minds
why.body1: A brand is not what you say about yourselves, it is what arrives with everyone else. That view of your own presence is the one you never get: you know the intent behind every sentence, a visitor only knows the sentence.
why.body2: The check takes that view. It does not judge your taste, it checks whether your intent makes it out — and every finding says what it rests on.

faq.title: What you want to know first
faq.q1A: Your homepage only: the visible text and the details in the page head, at most 20,000 characters. No login area, no subpages, no third-party data.
faq.q2A: We store the audited address, the score and the evidence so your result stays reachable under its link. The check needs no email address.
faq.q3A: Because that is where the brand decides: the homepage is the first impression. It is also the one place we can treat the same way on every website — only then are two results comparable at all.
faq.q4Q: How often may I run it?
faq.q4A: Three checks a day per connection. The same address returns the same stored result within seven days and does not count again.
faq.q5Q: Can I take my website out of the ranking?
faq.q5A: Yes. A check only enters the ranking with the checkbox, and anyone who runs a website can have its entry removed at any time — write to us and we hide it.
faq.q6A: Some things cannot be checked from the outside. Instead of guessing we mark them and leave them out of the calculation: they count neither as a point nor as a deduction.

checkMethod.seoDescription: What the Brand Score measures and what it does not: which page we read, how the {criteria} criteria in {categories} categories are scored, where the limits are, and how to have a result corrected or removed.
checkMethod.title: How we calculate
checkMethod.lead: This page explains how a Brand Score comes about. It exists because the brand check also rates presences that are not ours — and anyone who is rated has a right to redo the maths.
checkMethod.updated: It describes what is running today. If the calculation changes, this page changes with it.

what.title: What the Brand Score is
what.body: The Brand Score is a number between 0 and 100. It describes how clearly a publicly available web presence expresses its brand. The basis is the public self-presentation: the text every visitor sees, plus the technical declarations in the page head.
what.opinion: It is a classification, not a statement of fact — a reasoned opinion about how a presence comes across from the outside. Every single judgement carries its evidence from the presence itself, so that it can be contradicted.
what.not1: Not a statement about commercial success, revenue or solvency.
what.not2: Not a statement about the quality of the products or services behind it. Excellent craft can present itself badly — and the other way round.
what.not3: Not a statement about integrity or trustworthiness.
what.not4: Not a judgement of taste. We check whether a decision was recognisably made, not whether we like it.
what.bandsLead: The number turns into a word. The thresholds are fixed and apply to every result alike.

reads.title: What we read
reads.body: Exactly one page: the address that was entered, after all redirects. No crawling of the site, no second request.
reads.l1: The visible body text of that one page, at most {chars} characters. Anything beyond that is cut off and not scored.
reads.l2: The declarations in the page head: title, description, language, favicon, preview image, colour and appearance declarations, structured data, heading hierarchy.
reads.l3: The alt texts of images. We do not load the images themselves and we do not store them.
reads.l4: Whether the address leads to an encrypted connection.
reads.s1: No sub-pages. Whether an imprint, a contact or an about page is linked is something we see on that one page — we do not open it.
reads.s2: Nothing behind a login. We do not sign in anywhere and we do not fill in forms.
reads.s3: No social media profiles, no review sites, no registers, no press coverage.
reads.s4: No JavaScript. We read the document as delivered, not what a browser rebuilds from it.
reads.keepsBody: The page text is discarded after the evaluation. What remains stored is the checked address, the numeric values, the short pieces of evidence, the date, and a checksum of the text that tells us whether anything has changed since. Plus a daily rotating checksum of the requesting connection — for the daily cap only, never the address itself.
reads.agentTitle: How to recognise us in your access log
reads.robotsBody: Before we fetch a page we read your robots.txt and abide by it — including rules addressed to all bots. We also check for a machine-readable text and data mining reservation (§ 44b UrhG). If either forbids the evaluation, we stop: there is no score, no result and no stored entry — whoever started the check is told exactly that. Until 8 September 2026 this applied only to our market comparison; since then it applies here too.
reads.blockBody: Three ways, each effective with the next check. The first is one line in your robots.txt:
reads.tdmBody: The second way: we recognise a machine-readable reservation under § 44b UrhG in these four forms. One of them is enough:
reads.doubt: When in doubt we decide against the evaluation: if a reservation cannot be safely ruled out, we stop.
reads.blockContact: The third way needs no file: write to us and we will block your address on our side. That also applies retroactively to a result that already exists.
reads.limitBody: We ask the origin of the address that was entered. If it redirects to a different host, we do not additionally fetch that host’s robots.txt — our market comparison behaves the same way. And the website that a signed-in operator enters as their own in the brand wizard is still read without this preliminary request: there, the owner of the page is the one giving the order.

judge.title: How it is scored
judge.body: {criteria} criteria in {categories} categories. Every criterion has a fixed rule and awards 0, 1 or 2 points. The categories carry different weights; together they make up the {total} points of the overall score.

categories.distinctiveness: Does the presence say something only this brand could say — with a stance of its own instead of filler words?
categories.visual: Is a visual world of its own recognisable, and are the visible marks in place: favicon, preview image, heading hierarchy?
categories.consistency: Do title, heading and body speak with one voice, and is the brand name spelled the same way throughout?
categories.experience: Can a first-time visitor find their way: one clear next action, findable declarations, a recognisable sender?
categories.clarity: Does it say in plain words, without jargon, what is offered, for whom — and what is different here?
categories.emotion: Does the presence speak to a feeling: an origin, a human voice, a tone that fits the subject?
categories.adaptability: Does the brand carry elsewhere too: on a phone, in dark mode, in the sharing preview, in a single sentence?
categories.craft: Are the details right: spelling, no placeholder text, an encrypted connection, clean declarations in the page head?

judge.splitBody: {measured} of the {criteria} criteria are computed deterministically from the document — favicon, preview image, heading hierarchy, language declaration, encrypted connection and the like. The same page always yields the same points there. The remaining {judged} are judged by a language model, in one pass, with mandatory evidence for every judgement.
judge.modelTitle: Which model, and under which conditions
judge.modelBody: We call a large language model through a router — and only providers who have committed to not storing the request. Use for training purposes is prohibited, and falling back to providers outside those conditions is switched off: we would rather have the check say it is currently unavailable. Which model judged a given result is recorded with that result; it can change over time, which is why no fixed name is given here.
judge.varianceTitle: Why two runs can differ slightly
judge.varianceBody: The measured part is reproducible. The judged part almost is: we run the model as cold as possible, but a language model is not an adding machine. Above all the basis changes — today's website is not last week's. That is why every result carries its date, and why the same address deliberately returns the same stored result within {days} days instead of putting a second number next to the first.
judge.nullTitle: What cannot be checked from outside, we do not guess
judge.nullBody: A criterion about which nothing can honestly be said is marked not assessable and drops out of the calculation — it counts neither in the numerator nor in the denominator. Zero points would be a claim about something we never looked at.

maturity.title: Foundation maturity — the second number
maturity.body: Anyone building a branding with us can have their foundation checked instead of a website: the confirmed answers from the wizard. It is calculated with the same formula and the same catalogue of criteria.
maturity.labelBody: That is why this number has a different name and is labelled separately everywhere. The {measured} measured criteria are all not assessable there — a favicon and a heading hierarchy are properties of a page, not of a foundation. A foundation maturity of 78 and a website score of 78 say different things; the side-by-side view refuses to compare across that line.
maturity.note: Foundation maturity exists only for your own brand. It cannot be established for someone else's presence.

public.title: What is public — and what is not
public.privateTitle: A result is private to begin with
public.privateBody: A check enters our public ranking only if the person running it explicitly ticked the box at the start. Without that tick it appears in no list, no sorting and no ranking position.
public.linkBody: Every result gets its own shareable address. Anyone who knows it can open the result — it is meant to be passed on. Search engines do not index it, and it shows nothing that would not be public anyway: the checked address, and judgements about a publicly reachable page.
public.ownerTitle: We are aware that the person running a check is not always the brand owner
public.ownerBody: That is why there are two ways back. Both are free and need no account.
public.correctionBody: A correction can be submitted for any result: the field concerned, the suggestion, and a reason. A contact address is optional. We review by hand and either accept or decline with a reason. What can be corrected today is the industry — it is a model's suggestion about someone else's presence. The score itself is not contradicted by a correction, but through the route below.
public.removalBody: On a substantiated request we take a result offline. It disappears from the ranking and from its own address as well — what stands there afterwards is the same as for a result that never existed. The removal is permanent: it is not undone by someone else checking the same address again.
public.contactBody: For a correction the form on the result is enough. For a removal, to have your address blocked, or to query a judgement, write to us using the contact details in the imprint.

limits.title: Limits and fairness
limits.l1Body: The judged criteria are a machine judgement. It carries its evidence and is therefore verifiable, but it is not infallible. If you see a mistake, tell us.
limits.l2Body: It holds for one page on one day. A relaunch, a new text, a changed home page — and the number no longer holds. That is why every result carries its date, and why an old value is not a valid value to us.
limits.l3Title: We do not pit two brands against each other
limits.l3Body: There is a side-by-side view, but it is descriptive: two results next to each other, category by category, with no winner and no disparagement. We do not claim that one brand is better than another.
limits.l4Body: We show word marks, industry and short supporting quotes from the presence itself. No logos, no figurative marks, no favicons, no screenshots.
limits.l5Title: A home page is not the whole brand
limits.l5Body: A brand also lives in the product, in the shop, in conversation and in service. This check sees none of that. It measures the first impression online — that matters, but it is not everything.

note.mono: One ink, for embossing, stamps and engraving. There is no second colour here.
note.icon: A surface instead of paper: avatar, app icon, favicon.

note.wordmark: The full name, set in your heading typeface.
note.monogram: The initial in a tile — for everything small and square.

scene.title: In context

drafts.title: Stage 3 · AI drafts
drafts.intro: Generated from the briefing, the visual DNA and the colour world. These are IDEAS for the design work — not a finished logo, not checked, and no claim to protectability.

photo.title: Picture principles
photo.intro: Four axes decide everything that follows: light, crop, people and colour. They become the brief you send to your photographer.
photo.noPhotos: The sketches are drawn from your colour world, they are not photos. A sample picture would sell the very decision at stake here — you are choosing a principle, not a motif.

illustration.title: Illustration
illustration.intro: Is there illustration at all — and if so, in which language? "None" is a full answer, and the only rule nobody can break.

note.none: Photography and type carry everything — the simplest rule there is.
note.line: Fine outline drawings for origin and process — quiet, easy to extend.
note.area: Colour areas without outlines — poster-like, closer to packaging than to a manual.
note.organic: Drawn, irregular shapes — warm, but hard to keep consistent.

icons.title: Icons
icons.intro: The same five icons in three weights, with a probe drawn at the real stroke width. The only question here is whether the stroke sits with your body type.
icons.line: This is how an icon sits beside your body type.

note.regular: The same stroke weight as body type — quiet and unobtrusive.
note.fill: Filled: legible on small surfaces, reads as heavier.
note.bold: A thick stroke — loud, and very loud beside a serif.

rule.fits: It fits: {stroke} sits inside the range of your type ({family}: {range}).
rule.heavy: Heavier than your type: {stroke} is above the range ({family}: {range}). That is not a mistake, only louder — you can still confirm it.
rule.light: Finer than your type: {stroke} is below the range ({family}: {range}) — the icons disappear beside the line.
rule.area: An area has no stroke width. Beside {family} it reads as heavier than any line — check it at the smallest size you use.

dodont.title: Do & Don’t
dodont.tag: k.dodont · computed from your three decisions
dodont.intro: Six pairs: the four axes of your principle plus illustration and icons. Every do has its do-not — the pair is what makes the rule checkable.

tempo.title: Tempo
tempo.intro: Nobody reads a tempo, you see it. The three versions stand side by side and run at the same time — hit “Play the transition” and decide which one looks like you.

note.calm: Slow to start, gentle to settle. It reads as calm and certain — and a little unhurried.
note.lively: Shorter, with a slight overshoot: awake and friendly, but restless on long pages.
note.snappy: Almost no run-up. It reads as efficient and takes some of the calm out of the brand.

transitions.title: Transitions
transitions.intro: More tokens means more arguing in the team. Three are enough — they all hang on the tempo above and change with it. These exact names go into the manual and into the code.

scene.title: In the product
scene.intro: The same surface in the chosen tempo: cards fade in with an offset, the button reacts on hover. Light and dark you switch on the scene itself.
scene.note: Everything here runs on a base duration of {duration}. The switch above shows what people see who have set reduced motion in their operating system — the end state simply stands.

logo.title: Kinetic mark
logo.intro: Does your mark move? A yes costs one more file somebody has to maintain — and a version without movement. A no is a decision, not an omission.

note.no: The mark stands still — in an intro as well. It saves a file nobody would keep up to date.
note.yes: An 800 ms build for intros and loading screens. After that the mark stands; inside body copy it never moves.

rules.title: Motion rules
rules.intro: Six sentences, each one checkable on a real page. The last line always applies and cannot be switched off: reduced motion means the end state, not slow motion.

scene.heading: One sentence that says what you stand for.
scene.body: This is the paragraph visitors actually read: what you do, for whom — and why it looks like this and not otherwise.
scene.cardText: This is how surfaces on the background look: border, spacing and contrast all come from the same ramp.
scene.quote: A quote shows how the heading typeface runs across longer sentences.
scene.reducedMotion: Reduced motion is set — transitions stand still. Values: {duration} ms · {easing} · offset {stagger} ms.
